## Summary

Claim: people are forcing **Jev** into use cases it isn't built for, while overlooking its best current fit — **memory**. Jev can decide, in parallel before results ever enter the LLM's context:

- **recall** — what to retrieve
- **store** — what to write
- **merge** — what to fuse with existing entries
- **remove** — what to evict
- **relevance** — what actually deserves a context slot

The point is placement: these five decisions run as concurrent branches *upstream of context assembly*, so the model receives an already-curated memory view rather than raw dumps it must filter itself.

## Why it matters

- **Reframes Jev from runtime to substrate.** "Forcing Jev into use cases where it's not made for" implies its concurrency shape suits plumbing, not front-line use — the same "right tool, right layer" judgment as [[2026-09-14-rauchg-verifiers-skills-new-frameworks]] (verifiers/skills as harness-level primitives rather than library code).
- **Pre-context curation is the right chokepoint.** Deciding recall/relevance *before* context assembly is cheaper than having the model filter inside context — analogous to Julian's centralized-docs enforcement ([[2026-09-06-julian-risk-based-code-review]]): keep noise out of context mechanically instead of asking the LLM to ignore it.
- **Memory hygiene is a live problem for us.** Our own memory instructions require compressing what changes future decisions and pruning stale entries; the five-way split (recall/store/merge/remove/relevance) is a clean checklist for any agent-memory design review — directly relevant to the [[2026-09-14-manning-designing-ai-agents-book]] pattern-vocabulary evaluation.
- **Skepticism gates:** "Jev" is under-specified here — no repo link, no benchmark, and the claim "one of the best cases I can think of" is opinion from a tool author-adjacent voice. 35 replies but no visible like/bookmark signal (not exposed). Treat as a design lens, not an adoption recommendation.
